captions.text: A June evening in the south of Sweden, more than half a century ago: a tractor is coming home from the fields.
It runs on wood, with a thread of diesel.
One wood chip is stored dry in the barn, with thousands of others.
It was cut by the knives of a chipper.
The tractor carries it off to the field.
It rides on the roof rack, before dropping into the bunker.
The chip sinks gently, in about an hour.
It dries.
Then it blackens and falls apart.
It passes under a flame: a fire short of air, on purpose.
In a bed of red-hot charcoal, the gas cools and becomes fuel.
At the bottom, almost nothing is left.
The gas carries on, still very hot: it crosses a filter, then a cooler.
In the cylinder, that thread of diesel lights it.
On the test bench, forty kilowatts at the shaft: eighteen per cent, says the report.
So, by our sum, about two hundred and twenty kilowatts going in.
That evening, in the garage, the engine stops.
The gas does not stop with it: the last world is about that moment.
